claims.text: A nanometer-scale Nb interlayer between adjacent HEA layers will tune interface coherency.
Tuning coherency with an Nb interlayer will produce a controlled, gradual transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep.
Diffusion-mediated creep will dominate at higher temperatures, whereas dislocation-mediated creep will dominate at lower temperatures or higher stresses.
The initial HEA multilayers have coherent or semi-coherent interfaces.
A thin elemental Nb layer can be introduced between the HEA layers.
Coherency will be maintained at the HEA/Nb interfaces.
Nb has a close lattice match with many HEAs.
Nb's diffusivity and lattice match allow coherent HEA/Nb interfaces to form.
At elevated temperatures, the Nb layer enhances atomic diffusion along the interface.
Enhanced interfacial diffusion favors diffusion-controlled creep.
At lower temperatures or higher stresses, a coherent interface can support dislocation activity.
Dislocation activity at the HEA/Nb interface will favor dislocation-mediated creep.
Compared with multilayers lacking Nb, Nb-containing multilayers will exhibit a smoother and more predictable transition between creep mechanisms.
The mechanism transition will be observable through changes in creep strain rate and deformation mode.
HEA multilayers without an Nb transitional layer have a less controlled creep-mechanism transition and may develop nonuniform interfacial deformation.
The beneficial effect requires the Nb layer to remain thin enough to preserve coherent or semi-coherent interfaces.
An excessively thick Nb layer may cause interfacial discontinuities or phase mismatches that negate the proposed mechanism.
The optimal Nb thickness and effective temperature and stress windows are not yet determined.
